title: Head to Tail: Hox Genes, Retinoic Acid and Rhombomeres

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The embryonic {{c1::neural tube}} forms when the edges of the neural plate fold up and fuse.
cards.back: It becomes the brain and spinal cord.
cards.quote: The neural tube is the hollow rod that forms when the edges of the neural plate fold up and fuse.

cards.front: What are rhombomeres, and in which direction are they numbered?
cards.back: Small bulges of the early hindbrain, numbered r1 to r7 from front to back, with a less distinct r8 behind.
cards.quote: small bulges called rhombomeres, numbered r1 to r7 from front to back, with a less distinct r8 behind.

cards.front: In the chick hindbrain map, which rhombomere pairs produce motor neurons for cranial nerves V, VII and IX?
cards.back: r2–r3: trigeminal (V), jaw muscles. r4–r5: facial (VII), second-arch muscles. r6–r7: glossopharyngeal (IX), third-arch throat muscles. Each nerve exits from its pair’s even-numbered member.
cards.quote: The motor neurons of each cranial nerve came from a pair of rhombomeres.

cards.front: Suppose, in a chick experiment, clones labelled in the hindbrain before boundaries form sometimes cross them; equally large clones labelled after formation stay inside one segment. What does equal clone size help rule out?
cards.back: A simple failure of late cells to divide. Similar growth with restricted spread supports a boundary that confines progenitor descendants.
cards.quote: Clones labelled before boundaries appeared could span two rhombomeres. Clones labelled after boundaries formed stayed inside one.

cards.front: Why can rhombomeres be progenitor compartments even though some later neurons migrate across their boundaries?
cards.back: Compartment restriction describes progenitor lineages after boundaries form; it does not prohibit every later neuron from migrating across.
cards.quote: Some neurons born later do migrate across; the facial motor neurons of the mouse, met below, are one.

cards.front: In a fish hindbrain, contact repulsion between EphA4-positive cells and neighbouring ephrin-B-positive cells is blocked. What happens to sorting, and why?
cards.back: Sorting at those contacts should weaken because this repulsion helps keep the populations apart. Complete boundary loss is not established; contact repulsion is one mechanism.
cards.quote: In fish and frog embryos, r3 and r5 make the receptor EphA4, while their neighbours make ephrin-B ligands, and cells sort where the two meet.

cards.front: What does a transcription factor do?
cards.back: It switches other genes on and off.
cards.quote: The label is a set of transcription factors, proteins that switch other genes on and off.

cards.front: Why can Hoxa2 and Hoxb2 expression alone not distinguish early mouse r3 from r4?
cards.back: Both segments share them. Krox20 in r3 and later strong Hoxb1 in r4 distinguish their codes.
cards.quote: Rhombomeres r3 and r4 share Hoxa2 and Hoxb2, so those two cannot tell them apart.

cards.front: How do segment genes such as Krox20 and MafB help refine the early mouse hindbrain Hox code?
cards.back: They are transcription factors made in particular segments that switch on particular Hox genes: Krox20 in r3/r5 and MafB in r5/r6.
cards.quote: The segment genes are transcription factors too, each made in particular segments: Krox20 in r3 and r5, and MafB (Kreisler) in r5 and r6.

cards.front: In chick, a change at the midbrain–hindbrain signalling centre lets Hoxa2 enter r1. What does this show about the normal r1/r2 expression edge, and why?
cards.back: The edge is actively maintained: the normal boundary signal keeps Hoxa2 out of r1. Its position is not merely inherited from an earlier pattern.
cards.quote: a signal from the boundary between midbrain and hindbrain keeps Hoxa2 out of r1, and changing that signal changes where Hoxa2 is found.

cards.front: What directional rule links early retinoic acid to hindbrain identity, and what is its scope?
cards.back: Over the tested early range, more signal favours a posterior code and less an anterior code, for hindbrain Hox groups 1–4 before segments sharpen.
cards.why: The rule predicts direction, not exact edges or gene counts. Segment genes and local signals refine the code.
cards.quote: More early retinoic acid, a more posterior code; the code helps set the neurons.

cards.front: Where are normal mouse facial branchiomotor neurons born, and where do they form their motor nucleus?
cards.back: They are born in r4 and migrate backward to r6, forming the facial motor nucleus.
cards.quote: facial branchiomotor neurons are born in r4 and migrate backward to r6, where they form the facial motor nucleus.

cards.front: Why does Hoxb1 loss make mouse r4 closer to r2 rather than simply converting it to r3?
cards.back: Hoxb1 normally helps maintain Hoxb2, which also drops in mutant r4. r4 lacks Krox20, so deleting Hoxb1 does not recreate the r3 network.
cards.quote: Hoxb1 helps keep Hoxb2 on in r4, so in the mutant Hoxb2 drops there too.

cards.front: A mouse lacks Hoxb1 but retains r4 progenitors. What happens to facial movement, and why?
cards.back: Weak or absent facial movement is predicted: r4 loses its normal facial neuron program, and a working facial motor nucleus and nerve VII motor supply fail.
cards.quote: Without a working facial motor nucleus, the muscles of facial expression lose their motor supply, so you would predict weak or absent facial movement.

cards.front: Deleting a hypothetical patterning gene leaves an embryonic segment present and dividing, but its motor neurons adopt a neighbouring segment’s program. What role does the deletion support?
cards.back: A role in segment identity. The retained segment still produces motor neurons; the change concerns their program rather than simple loss of the territory.
cards.quote: Its progenitors still divide, and they still make motor neurons, now with a different identity.

cards.front: Why does the failure of r3 and r5 to persist in Krox20-null mice not establish that all their cells died?
cards.back: Fate mapping shows some cells survive, mix with neighbours and adopt even-numbered segment identities. Recognizable territory can disappear without deletion of all its cells.
cards.quote: Fate mapping shows that some Krox20-lacking cells survive, mix with neighbours and take on the identity of even-numbered segments.

cards.front: A transcription factor’s expression matches an embryonic region. How would you test whether it helps cause regional identity, and what would a positive result still leave unresolved?
cards.back: Disrupt the factor and assess both tissue persistence and cell identity. A retained region making different neurons supports necessity for identity. By the expression-versus-knockout logic, it still does not establish that the factor works alone.
cards.quote: Either way, the code acts as a cause, not just a marker.

cards.front: Through which intermediate is retinoic acid made from retinol, and how many oxidations are involved?
cards.back: Retinol (vitamin A) passes through retinaldehyde to retinoic acid in two oxidations.
cards.quote: Retinoic acid is made from retinol (vitamin A) in two oxidations, through retinaldehyde.
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: How do Raldh2 and Cyp26 help create the early hindbrain retinoic acid gradient?
cards.back: Raldh2 supplies retinoic acid beside the posterior hindbrain; Cyp26 enzymes destroy it, with Cyp26a1 strong anteriorly. Supply behind and destruction ahead favour a posterior-high gradient.
cards.quote: Supply behind and destruction in front leave retinoic acid high toward the back of the hindbrain and low toward the front.
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: How can retinoic acid reach receptors in the nucleus without first activating a cell-surface receptor?
cards.back: It is small and oily, so it crosses membranes and reaches the nucleus.
cards.quote: Retinoic acid is small and oily, so it crosses membranes and reaches the nucleus.
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: Which receptor pair reads retinoic acid at DNA response elements?
cards.back: RAR, which binds retinoic acid, works with RXR at retinoic acid response elements (RAREs). Hoxa1 and Hoxb1 carry RAREs.
cards.quote: the retinoic acid receptor (RAR), which works as a pair with the retinoid X receptor (RXR)
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: In a simple activation-threshold model, signal exposure falls below gene B’s threshold but stays above gene A’s. What happens to their activation, and why?
cards.back: A remains activated while B loses activation because only A’s threshold is met. This uses the simple threshold rule; additional regulatory inputs can change real patterns.
cards.quote: In cell culture, 3′ Hox genes respond to lower doses of retinoic acid than 5′ genes.
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: Early retinoic acid exposure in mouse embryos gives r2 and r3 features of r4 and r5. What happened to regional identity, and which way did the Hox domains move?
cards.back: Anterior segments shifted toward posterior identities as Hox domains extended forward. This shows the effect of excess early signal, not by itself the normal signal’s role.
cards.quote: The edges should move forward, so the front segments carry a code that normally sits farther back.
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: An early embryonic signal is supplied posteriorly and destroyed anteriorly. Anterior destruction is reduced while supply stays constant. What happens to anterior signal exposure, and why?
cards.back: It should increase and persist farther forward because the anterior drain is weaker. This follows the source-and-destruction rule used for retinoic acid.
cards.quote: Retinoic acid should persist farther forward, so the front of the hindbrain should shift toward a more posterior character.
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: Extra retinoic acid changes an embryo’s pattern. Why does blocking its synthesis provide different evidence about normal development?
cards.back: Synthesis loss tests whether the normal signal is needed; excess exposure only shows the response to too much. Loss of posterior pattern after synthesis blockade supports normal necessity.
cards.quote: Blocking synthesis like this is the better guide to what the normal signal does.
cards.section: Where the edges come from: a tap at the back, a drain at the front

cards.front: Why can a model in which retinoic acid only switches genes on not explain the later narrow Hoxb1 domain in mouse r4?
cards.back: It predicts expression from a threshold edge all the way back. Feedback loops and repression, including a second RARE, help confine Hoxb1 to r4.
cards.quote: A threshold rule in which retinoic acid only switches genes on predicts that each gene stays on from its edge all the way back.

cards.front: A graded signal could encode position through concentration or exposure duration. How would you distinguish these explanations experimentally?
cards.back: Compare equal-duration exposures at different concentrations, then equal-concentration exposures of different durations; measure downstream expression over time. The rule is that both signal amount and exposure time could affect the pattern.
cards.quote: Whether cells read how much signal they get or how long they get it is still argued

cards.front: An agent that causes birth defects after embryonic or fetal exposure is a {{c1::teratogen}}.
cards.back: Retinoids are an example.
cards.quote: A teratogen is an agent that causes birth defects when an embryo or fetus is exposed to it.

cards.front: What is the proposed link between early retinoid exposure and human birth defects, and how direct is the mechanistic evidence?
cards.back: Animal work shows altered hindbrain Hox codes and disturbed face-building neural crest cells. This mechanism is inferred in humans, rather than directly demonstrated in human embryos.
cards.quote: In human embryos this mechanism is inferred from the animal work rather than shown directly

cards.front: An embryo receives far too little vitamin A instead of excess retinoic acid. Does this remove the risk of developmental harm, and why?
cards.back: No. Too little vitamin A also harms development because the embryo needs the normal signal; both deficiency and excess can disturb patterning.
cards.quote: Too little vitamin A harms the embryo as well. The dose has to be right in both directions.

cards.front: The homeobox encodes the DNA-binding {{c1::homeodomain}} of a protein.
cards.back: Hox genes are one branch of the larger homeobox family.
cards.quote: It encodes the homeodomain, a part of the protein that later work showed binds DNA
cards.section: Order on the chromosome, order along the body

cards.front: How are the 39 Hox genes in mice and humans organized into clusters?
cards.back: Four clusters, Hoxa, Hoxb, Hoxc and Hoxd, each on a different chromosome; no cluster contains all 13 paralog groups.
cards.quote: Mice and humans have 39, in four clusters called Hoxa, Hoxb, Hoxc and Hoxd, each on a different chromosome.
cards.section: Order on the chromosome, order along the body

cards.front: What is a Hox paralog group, and why can it make a single-gene knockout milder than expected?
cards.back: It groups genes at matching positions in different clusters. Their similar sequences and often similar expression allow partial substitution for a missing gene.
cards.quote: Paralogs have similar sequences and often similar expression, so they can stand in for one another
cards.section: Order on the chromosome, order along the body

cards.front: A vertebrate Hox cluster has genes near its 3′ and 5′ ends. A student predicts that the 5′ gene activates first and reaches farther anteriorly. What should change, and why?
cards.back: Reverse both predictions: the 3′ gene generally activates earlier and reaches farther anteriorly. Spatial and temporal colinearity support this trend, with local boundary exceptions.
cards.quote: Genes farther toward the 5′ end have edges farther back, and group 13 is expressed near the tail.
cards.section: Order on the chromosome, order along the body

cards.front: How do spatial and temporal Hox colinearity differ in vertebrates?
cards.back: Spatial: 3′ genes generally reach farther anteriorly than 5′ genes. Temporal: in mouse and chick, 3′ genes turn on before 5′ genes as the axis grows backward.
cards.quote: In mouse and chick, 3′ genes are also switched on first and 5′ genes later, as the body axis grows backward.
cards.section: Order on the chromosome, order along the body

cards.front: In the early mouse code, why does the Hoxb2 front edge at r3, ahead of Hoxb1 at r4, not overturn whole-body spatial colinearity?
cards.back: Colinearity is a whole-body trend, not a rule for every boundary. Other inputs help set group 2 edges in the hindbrain.
cards.quote: Colinearity is a trend along the whole body, not a law for every boundary.
cards.section: Order on the chromosome, order along the body

cards.front: A different embryonic axis has a signal source and a distant degradation zone. How could you test whether the proposed gradient helps set regional identity?
cards.back: Map signal activity and regional transcription factors, then separately reduce supply and degradation and assess identity. The source-and-destruction rule predicts opposed signal changes; coupled identity changes would support a patterning role.
cards.quote: Signals that spread from a source, and are destroyed or opposed elsewhere, form graded concentrations, and those gradients help set the pattern.
cards.section: What this example teaches about every axis

cards.front: How would you strengthen the claim that the embryo’s own retinoic acid gradient instructs position rather than merely being needed for development?
cards.back: Control where and when the signal acts, then measure Hox expression and regional neuronal identity. The rule is that necessity and altered identity suggest instruction, but identifying positional information requires spatial and temporal control.
cards.quote: Showing which features of the embryo's own gradient carry position would need experiments that control where and when the signal acts.

cards.front: Extra Cyp26 acts only in the posterior hindbrain during early patterning. What happens to posterior neuronal programs, and can every Hox edge be assigned an equal displacement?
cards.back: A shift toward anterior neuronal programs is predicted, not established. The rule is less retinoic acid favours an anterior code, which helps set neurons. Equal edge shifts are not guaranteed: profile shape and local regulation matter.
cards.quote: By the rule, posterior segments should shift toward a more anterior identity, the direction seen when Raldh2 or vitamin A is lacking.

cards.front: After hindbrain patterning is perturbed, a segment marker vanishes. How would you distinguish identity change, mixing and cell death?
cards.back: Combine tissue boundaries and width with independent markers, lineage tracing, and dividing/dying-cell counts; assess neuronal programs if tissue persists. The rule is that loss of a recognizable territory or marker alone does not identify the fate of its cells.
cards.quote: Cells may have changed identity, mixed with neighbours or died.

cards.front: What are the three primary vesicles of the early brain, with their formal names?
cards.back: Forebrain: prosencephalon. Midbrain: mesencephalon. Hindbrain: rhombencephalon.
cards.quote: The three vesicles have formal names: the forebrain (prosencephalon), the midbrain (mesencephalon) and the hindbrain (rhombencephalon).
cards.section: The regions of the early tube

cards.front: What are the forebrain’s two subdivisions, and which major structures do they produce?
cards.back: Telencephalon: cerebral hemispheres. Diencephalon: thalamus and neighbours, plus optic vesicles that become the retinas.
cards.quote: the telencephalon, which makes the cerebral hemispheres, and the diencephalon, which makes the thalamus and its neighbours
cards.section: The regions of the early tube

cards.front: Which subdivisions of the hindbrain produce the pons, cerebellum and medulla?
cards.back: Metencephalon: pons and cerebellum. Myelencephalon: medulla.
cards.quote: The hindbrain divides into the metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) and the myelencephalon (medulla).
cards.section: The regions of the early tube
